results.question: Is there a waiting period before I can get the general social security benefit?
results.answer:
Yes, you generally must complete a 7-working-day waiting period before receiving the general social security benefit [S2]. 

You cannot get the benefit during this waiting period [S2]. The period is met once you have been registered as an unemployed jobseeker with employment services for at least 7 working days [S2]. If you work part-time, your waiting period is calculated by deducting your worked hours from the maximum collective agreement hours until they amount to 7 full working days [S2]. 

You do not need to complete a new waiting period if you transition directly from earnings-related unemployment allowance to the general social security benefit [S2][S5]. Holiday compensation periodisation may postpone when your waiting period begins [S8].

results.question: I have no vocational qualification. Do I have to wait longer before I get the general social security benefit?
results.answer: If you do not have a vocational qualification or a higher education degree, you must complete a qualifying period (odotusaika) before you can receive the general social security benefit [S1]. The maximum length of this qualifying period is 21 weeks [S3]. Upper secondary school education (lukio) and the matriculation examination do not count as a vocational qualification [S1][S4]. This qualifying period applies to jobseekers of all ages [S1]. Additionally, if you are under 25, you must apply for admission to at least two education programmes to qualify for the benefit [S8].

results.question: How does part-time work affect my general social security benefit?
results.answer:
Part-time work will reduce the amount of general social security benefit you receive, as Kela pays you an adjusted benefit [S5]. 

The basic rule is that your benefit is reduced by 50 cents for every euro you earn in wages or salary [S8]. Your income affects the benefit during the specific payment period in which the wages are actually paid to you, regardless of when you earned them [S1][S8]. 

To qualify for the adjusted benefit, your working hours must be up to 80% of full-time hours in your industry, there must be no full-time work available, and you must stay registered as a jobseeker while looking for full-time work [S4]. You cannot get the adjusted benefit if you work fewer hours on your own initiative [S4].

results.question: Can income other than wages reduce my general social security benefit?
results.answer:
Yes, other income besides wages or salary can reduce your general social security benefit because the benefit is means-tested [S1][S3]. 

Types of income that can reduce your benefit include capital income, informal care allowances, partial early old-age pensions, compensations for family caregivers, and copyright royalties [S3]. Kela takes these incomes into account at their gross amount [S2]. 

You can receive up to EUR 311 per month in capital income or other non-wage income without it affecting your benefit [S4]. If this income exceeds EUR 311 per month, 50% of the amount exceeding the limit will be deducted from your general social security benefit [S4].
